Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and visualization library(tidymodels) # modeling ``` ::: ## Today's data {.smaller} 2026 House results and projections from Decision Desk HQ (as of 2026-11-04, 11:14 am), merged with 2024 results (from the `gerrymander` dataset we worked with earlier in the semester): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} midterm_26_raw <- read_csv("data/midterm-2026-11-04-11-14.csv") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(midterm_26_raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 443 Columns: 18 $ district "AK-00", "AL-01", "AL-02", "AL-03", "AL-04", "AL-05", "… $ state_abb "AK", "AL", "AL", "AL", "AL", "AL", "AL", "AL", "AR", "… $ state "Alaska", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "… $ house_rep_20 "Don Young", "Jerry Carl", "Barry Moore", "Mike Rogers"… $ house_party_20 "Republican", "Republican", "Republican", "Republican",… $ house_rep_22 "Mary Sattler Peltola", "Jerry L Carl", "Barry Moore", … $ house_party_22 "Democrat", "Republican", "Republican", "Republican", "… $ house_rep_24 "Nick Begich", "Barry Moore", "Shomari Figures", "Mike … $ house_party_24 "Republican", "Republican", "Democrat", "Republican", "… $ harris_24 41.41, 21.89, 53.52, 26.18, 15.96, 34.20, 29.68, 61.45,… $ trump_24 54.54, 76.94, 45.31, 72.71, 83.02, 64.02, 68.47, 37.50,… $ gerry_22 NA, "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "C", "C", "C", "… $ gerry_24 NA, "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "… $ gerry_26 NA, "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "… $ rating_26 "Lean R", "Safe R", "Lean R", "Safe R", "Safe R", "Safe… $ leader_26 "Republican", "Republican", "Democrat", "Republican", "… $ margin_26 9.00, 18.00, 8.00, 28.00, 50.00, 7.00, 15.00, 39.00, 35… $ called_26 "uncalled", "called", "called", "called", "called", "ca… ``` ::: ::: ## Data prep {.smaller} - A seat flips to Democrat if it was held by a Republican after 2024 and a Democrat leads in 2026: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # fmt: skip midterm_26 <- midterm_26_raw |> mutate( flip_dem_24_26 = case_when( called_26 == "uncalled" ~ NA, called_26 == "called" & house_party_24 == "Republican" & leader_26 == "Democrat" ~ "1", called_26 == "called" & house_party_24 == "Republican" & leader_26 == "Republican" ~ "0", called_26 == "called" & house_party_24 == "Democrat" ~ "0", ), flip_dem_24_26 = as.factor(flip_dem_24_26) ) |> filter(!is.na(called_26)) ``` ::: - Data split: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} midterm_26_called <- midterm_26 |> filter(called_26 == "called") midterm_26_uncalled <- midterm_26 |> filter(called_26 == "uncalled") ``` ::: ## Goal {.smaller} Predict whether a seat flips to Democrat based on Trump's 2024 vote share for uncalled seats, using data from called seats. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot( midterm_26, aes(x = trump_24, y = flip_dem_24_26, fill = flip_dem_24_26) ) + geom_jitter( shape = "circle filled", height = 0.2, alpha = 0.7, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE, color = "white" ) + scale_fill_manual( values = c("0" = "darkgray", "1" = "#0015BC"), na.value = "#A3B18A" ) + scale_x_continuous( limits = c(10, 90), breaks = seq(0, 100, 10), labels = label_percent(scale = 1) ) + labs( x = "Trump's 2024 vote share (%)", y = "Flipped to Democrat", title = "2026 House elections", caption = "Data from Decision Desk HQ, as of 2026-11-04 at 11:14 am" ) + facet_wrap(~called_26, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/flip-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Fitting a logistic model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flip_fit <- logistic_reg() |> fit(flip_dem_24_26 ~ trump_24, data = midterm_26_called) tidy(flip_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) -3.48 0.648 -5.37 0.0000000805 2 trump_24 0.0244 0.0117 2.08 0.0372 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .fragment} ## Remember In logistic regression, we predict the log odds of the probability of success, $\log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right)$. ::: ## Output $\rightarrow$ model - Output ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(flip_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) -3.48 0.648 -5.37 0.0000000805 2 trump_24 0.0244 0.0117 2.08 0.0372 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Fitted model: $$ \log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right) = -3.48 + 0.0244\times trump\_24 $$ ## The intercept {.smaller} - If `trump_24 = 0`, then $$ \begin{aligned} \log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right) &= b_0 + b_1 \times 0 \\ &= b_0 \\ \end{aligned} $$ . . . - Exponentiating both sides: $$ \begin{aligned} e^{\log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right)} &= e^{b_0} \\ \frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}} &= e^{b_0} \end{aligned} $$ ## Interpreting the intercept {.smaller} $$ \log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right) = -3.48 + 0.0244\times trump\_24 $$
. . . $$ e^{-3.48} = 0.03 $$ . . . - Seats where Trump got 0% of the vote in 2024 are predicted, on average, to have a 3% odds of flipping to Democrat. - Since Trump's vote share in called seats ranges from 10.6% to 83%, so this is an extrapolation and not meaningful. ## The slope I 1. Find log odds when the predictor is equal to $x$: $$ log(odds_1) = {b_0} + {b_1x} $$ . . . 2. Increase $x$ by one unit and find log odds when the predictor is equal to $x + 1$: $$ log(odds_2) = {b_0} + {b_1(x + 1)} $$ ## The slope II {.smaller} Difference between the two log odds: $$ \begin{aligned} log(odds_2) - log(odds_1) &= ({b_0} + {b_1 (x + 1)}) - ({b_0} + {b_1x}) \\ log\Big(\frac{odds_2}{odds_1}\Big) &= b_0 + b_1x + b_1 - b_0 - b_1x \\ log\Big(\frac{odds_2}{odds_1}\Big) &= b_1 \end{aligned} $$ ## The slope III {.smaller} Difference between the odds, by exponentiating both sides: $$ \begin{aligned} log\Big(\frac{odds_2}{odds_1}\Big) &= b_1 \\ \frac{odds_2}{odds_1} &= e^{b_1} \end{aligned} $$ ## Interpreting the slope {.smaller} $$ \log\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\right) = -3.48 + 0.0244\times trump\_24 $$
. . . $$ e^{0.0244} \approx 1.02 $$ . . . Seats where Trump's 2024 vote share was one percentage point higher are predicted to have **odds** of flipping to Democrat that are **higher** by a factor of $e^{0.0244}\approx 1.02$, on average. # Classification
(prediction by another name...) ## Predict {.smaller} ::: question How well did our model do for predicting already called house seats? ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} midterm_26_called_aug <- augment(flip_fit, new_data = midterm_26_called) midterm_26_called_aug |> count(flip_dem_24_26, .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 flip_dem_24_26 .pred_class n 1 0 0 353 2 1 0 38 ``` ::: ::: Terrible! ::: ::: {.question .fragment} Is that surprising? ::: ## Predict for uncalled seats {.smaller .scrollable} ::: {.cell} ```{.r and render, commit, and push your edits by the end of class. ::: # Spending your data ## Data - Taxi trips in Chicago, IL in 2022 - Data from [Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org/Transportation/Taxi-Trips/wrvz-psew) ## Data: `chicago_taxi` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chicago_taxi <- read_csv("data/chicago-taxi.csv") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chicago_taxi ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,000 × 7 tip distance company local dow month hour 1 no 0.4 other yes Fri Mar 17 2 no 0.96 Taxicab Insurance Agency Llc no Mon Apr 8 3 no 1.07 Sun Taxi no Fri Feb 15 4 no 1.13 other no Sat Feb 14 5 no 10.8 Sun Taxi no Sat Apr 14 6 no 3.6 Chicago Independents no Wed Mar 12 7 no 1.08 Flash Cab yes Wed Mar 13 8 no 0.85 Taxicab Insurance Agency Llc no Tue Mar 8 9 no 17.9 City Service no Tue Jan 20 10 no 0 City Service yes Sun Apr 16 # ℹ 1,990 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Data: `chicago_taxi` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(chicago_taxi) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 2,000 Columns: 7 $ tip "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "… $ distance 0.40, 0.96, 1.07, 1.13, 10.81, 3.60, 1.08, 0.85, 17.92, 0.00,… $ company "other", "Taxicab Insurance Agency Llc", "Sun Taxi", "other",… $ local "yes", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "yes", "no", "no", "yes"… $ dow "Fri", "Mon", "Fri", "Sat", "Sat", "Wed", "Wed", "Tue", "Tue"… $ month "Mar", "Apr", "Feb", "Feb", "Apr", "Mar", "Mar", "Mar", "Jan"… $ hour 17, 8, 15, 14, 14, 12, 13, 8, 20, 16, 20, 8, 15, 15, 12, 0, 1… ``` ::: ::: ## Data prep ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chicago_taxi <- chicago_taxi |> mutate( tip = fct_relevel(tip, "no", "yes"), local = fct_relevel(local, "no", "yes"), dow = fct_relevel(dow, "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"), month = fct_relevel(month, "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr") ) ``` ::: ## Outcome and predictors {.smaller} - Outcome - `tip`: Whether rider left a tip -- a factor w/ levels "yes" and "no" - (Potential) predictors: - Numerical: - `distance`: The trip distance, in odometer miles. - `hour`: The hour of the day in which the trip began. - Categorical: - `company`: The taxi company -- companies that occurred few times were binned as "other". - `local`: Whether the trip started in the same community area as it began. - `dow`: The day of the week in which the trip began. - `month`: The month in which the trip began. ## Should we include a predictor? To determine whether we should include a predictor in a model, we should start by asking: ::: incremental - Is it ethical to use this variable? (Or even legal?) - Will this variable be available at prediction time? - Does this variable contribute to explainability? ::: # Data splitting and spending ## We've been cheating! ::: incremental - So far, we've been using all the data we have for building models. In predictive contexts, this would be considered *cheating*. - Evaluating model performance for predicting outcomes that were used when building the models is like evaluating your learning with questions whose answers you've already seen. ::: ## Spending your data {.smaller} For predictive models (used primarily in machine learning), we typically split data into training and test sets: ![](images/20/test-train-split-1.svg){fig-align="center"} - The **training set** is used to estimate model parameters. - The **test set** is used to find an independent assessment of model performance. . . . ::: callout-warning Do not use, or even peek at, the test set during training. ::: ## How much to spend? ::: incremental - The more data we spend (use in training), the better estimates we’ll get. - Spending too much data in training prevents us from computing a good assessment of predictive performance. - Spending too much data in testing prevents us from computing a good estimate of model parameters. ::: ## The initial split ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(20261108) chicago_taxi_split <- initial_split(chicago_taxi) chicago_taxi_split ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` <1500/500/2000> ``` ::: ::: ## Setting a seed {.smaller} ::: task What does `set.seed()` do? ::: ::: incremental - To create that split of the data, R generates “pseudo-random” numbers: while they are made to behave like random numbers, their generation is deterministic given a “seed”. - This allows us to reproduce results by setting that seed. - Which seed you pick doesn’t matter, as long as you don’t try a bunch of seeds and pick the one that gives you the best performance. ::: ## Accessing the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chicago_taxi_train <- training(chicago_taxi_split) chicago_taxi_test <- testing(chicago_taxi_split) ``` ::: ## The training set {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chicago_taxi_train ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1,500 × 7 tip distance company local dow month hour 1 yes 12.0 Flash Cab no Tue Jan 13 2 no 0.03 City Service yes Sat Apr 22 3 no 7.66 Sun Taxi no Thu Feb 14 4 yes 1.57 other no Thu Feb 18 5 no 6.26 Flash Cab no Wed Feb 9 6 yes 18.0 City Service no Thu Mar 19 7 yes 0.75 Sun Taxi no Mon Feb 10 8 yes 1.31 Sun Taxi no Sun Feb 14 9 yes 17.5 City Service no Wed Feb 7 10 yes 9.95 City Service no Sun Jan 19 # ℹ 1,490 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## The testing data . . . ::: huge 🙈 ::: # Exploratory data analysis ## Initial questions {.smaller} - What's the distribution of the outcome, `tip`? - What's the distribution of numeric variables like `distance` or `hour`? - How does the distribution of `tip` differ across the categorical and numerical variables? ## Participate 📱💻 {.xsmall} ::: columns ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: wooclap Which dataset should we use for the exploration? ::: wooclap-choices - The entire data `chicago_taxi` - The training data `chicago_taxi_train` - The testing data `chicago_taxi_test` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ![](images/20/wooclap-qr.png){width="200" fig-align="center" fig-alt="QR code for Wooclap"} Go to [wooclap.com](https://app.wooclap.com/OMEXALN) and use the code OMEXALN. ::: ::: ## `tip` What’s the distribution of the outcome, `tip`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} chicago_taxi_train |> count(tip) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 tip n prop 1 no 571 0.381 2 yes 929 0.619 ``` ::: ::: ## `distance` What’s the distribution of `distance`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(chicago_taxi_train, aes(x = distance)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## `tip` and `distance` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(chicago_taxi_train, aes(x = distance, fill = tip, group = tip)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("yes" = "darkolivegreen4", "no" = "darkgray")) + facet_wrap(~tip, ncol = 1, labeller = label_both, scales = "free_y") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## `tip` and `hour` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(chicago_taxi_train, aes(x = hour, fill = tip, group = tip)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("yes" = "darkolivegreen4", "no" = "darkgray")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 18, by = 6)) + facet_wrap(~tip, ncol = 1, labeller = label_both, scales = "free_y") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## `tip` and `local` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|2"} ggplot(chicago_taxi_train, aes(x = local, fill = tip)) + geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("yes" = "darkolivegreen4", "no" = "darkgray")) + labs(y = "Proportion") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## `tip` and `dow` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(chicago_taxi_train, aes(x = dow, fill = tip)) + geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("yes" = "darkolivegreen4", "no" = "darkgray")) + labs(y = "Proportion", x = "Day of week") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](20-spending-your-data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Terminology ## False negative and positive - **False negative rate** is the proportion of actual positives that were classified as negatives. - **False positive rate** is the proportion of actual negatives that were classified as positives. ## Sensitivity **Sensitivity** is the proportion of actual positives that were correctly classified as positive. - Also known as **true positive rate** and **recall** - Sensitivity = 1 − False negative rate - Useful when false negatives are more "expensive" than false positives ## Specificity **Specificity** is the proportion of actual negatives that were correctly classified as negative - Also known as **true negative rate** - Specificity = 1 − False positive rate ## ROC curve ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} The **receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve** allows to assess the model performance across a range of thresholds. ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ![](images/20/roc-curve.png) ::: ::: ## Participate 📱💻 {.xsmall} ::: columns ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: wooclap Which of the following best describes the area annotated on the ROC curve? ![](images/20/roc-curve-annotated-question.png){width="350" fig-align="center"} ::: wooclap-choices - Where all positives classified as positive, all negatives classified as negative - Where true positive rate = false positive rate - Where all positives classified as negative, all negatives classified as positive ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ![](images/20/wooclap-qr.png){width="200" fig-align="center" fig-alt="QR code for Wooclap"} Go to [wooclap.com](https://app.wooclap.com/OMEXALN) and use the code OMEXALN. ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
